opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think shopping is actually one of my favorite personal use cases, and it's kind of funny because it's not what we originally built it for. But the reason it works so well is that finding clothing is a really long-tail, specific search problem. Usually I have something quite particular in mind, like a certain cut, a certain fabric, a price range, maybe I want it from a smaller brand that isn't one of the big names. And if you try to do that with a normal search engine, you end up opening dozens of tabs, scrolling through pages of results, and a lot of it is just SEO-optimized listicles that aren't very helpful.

With Deep Research, I can just describe exactly what I want, with all the constraints, and it'll go off and browse a ton of different sites, including smaller brands I've never heard of, and come back with options that actually match. It's really good at discovery in that way. It surfaces things I wouldn't have found myself because I wouldn't have known what to search for.

And it's also good at the tedious verification parts, like checking whether something is actually in stock, what sizes are available, what the materials are, reading reviews. Those are all things I'd do manually, and it takes a long time, so it's nice to hand that off and come back ten minutes later to a nicely organized report.

I think more generally that's the kind of task where it shines: anything where you'd otherwise spend hours doing a lot of searching and synthesizing information across many sources. Shopping just happens to be a really relatable example of that.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is kind of a funny use case, but it's actually one of my favorites. The thing about shopping, especially for clothes, is that it's a really hard search problem. If I know exactly what I want, like a specific brand and a specific item, then Google is great. But most of the time that's not the situation I'm in. I'll have something pretty specific in my head, like I want a particular style of jacket, in a particular material, in a certain price range, and I want it from a brand that's maybe smaller or more independent, not one of the big ones I already know about. And that's really hard to search for with a normal search engine, because you'd have to go through so many different sites, look at a lot of product pages, and compare things yourself.

What Deep Research is good at is exactly that kind of task. I can describe what I'm looking for in natural language, with all the constraints, and it will go off and browse a bunch of different websites, find brands I've never heard of, look at the actual products, and come back with a report of options that match what I asked for. It does the tedious part of the search for me. And I've genuinely found brands through it that I now buy from, which I don't think I would have discovered otherwise.

I think it's also a nice example of the broader thing we were going for with the product. It's not just answering a question from what the model already knows. It's doing the kind of multi-step browsing and synthesis that a person would do if they had a few hours to spend on it, and most of us don't want to spend a few hours finding a jacket.

r001.rationale: The response says Deep Research handles clothing searches with several constraints better than a normal search engine, but it does not clearly compare it with standard models.

astra-6.text: Fashion is surprisingly hard to search for when you have something specific in mind but don’t know which brand makes it. You might know the silhouette, the material, the color, and your budget, but getting all of those constraints into a normal search is difficult. Deep Research is useful because you can describe what you’re looking for in natural language and have it look across lots of brands. And the discovery part is really nice—you can find smaller brands you wouldn’t have known to search for in the first place.

sol-6.1.text:
I think fashion is surprisingly hard to search for. You might have a very specific idea of what you want—the cut, the fabric, the color—but not know the brand or even the right words to describe it. And there are so many smaller brands that you’d never discover just by going to the same few websites.

With Deep Research, I can describe what I’m looking for, give it constraints, and have it look across a bunch of different sites. It’s useful both for discovering brands that fit my taste and for finding a particular piece without having to open dozens of tabs myself.

r001.rationale: The response says Deep Research can take constraints and search across sites, but does not compare it with standard models or say it is better at satisfying multiple simultaneous constraints.

r002.rationale: It does not mention standard models, current-season availability, or lack of up-to-date information.
